A Family Affair BY JODY DUNCAN etween Avengers Tony 'Iron Man' Stark and Steve 'Captain America' Rogers there has always been a current of tension running beneath the characters' mutual respect and friendship - a bristling perhaps inevitable given the former's inherent cynicism and the latter's inherent earnestness. That tension erupts into war, superhero style, in Captain America: Civil War, the latest Marvel Studios production, directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, veterans of Marvel's previous Captain America: Winter Soldier. Other returnees to the Marvel universe were Winter Soldier visual effects supervisor Dan DeLeeuw and visual effects producer Jen Underdahl who, with visual effects associate supervisor Swen Gillberg, oversaw a four-person in-house team and 15 visual effects companies, all of which collaborated to deliver nearly 3,000 visual effects shots. Though replete with the super-charged action hardwired into all comic book-inspired films, Captain America: Civil War has a storyline that is serious in tone, as the Avengers grapple with a central question: Tallying up the destruction left in their wake - in Sokovia, New York City and elsewhere - are they doing more harm than good? On one side 1 / 41 of that conflict is Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.), who agrees to proposed governmental

CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 oversight of the Avengers' actions; on the other side is Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), determined that the Avengers maintain their autonomy. "The Winter Soldier was more of a '70s spy thriller," said Dan DeLeeuw. "It was a much brighter film. Moving into this one, we knew it was going to be a more serious movie, more of a mood piece. It's a family fight, essentially - except the family members are all superheroes." "This movie took on a much more character-driven, emotional tone," affirmed Jen Underdahl.iIt was supported by a lot of visual effects - with all of the spectacle that you would expect in a superhero movie - but then there are these deep, intense, characterdriven moments, as well." As always with a Marvel production, the studio's visual development department, led by Ryan Meinderding, served as incubator for the film's look, spending months prior to principal photography generating designs for both returning Avengers and those new to the fold. On Iron Man's team: veterans Black Widow (Scarlett Johansson), War Machine (Don Cheadle) and Vision (Paul Bettany), joined by new characters Black Panther (Chadwick Boseman) and Spider-Man (Tom Holland). On Captain America's team: Winter Soldier (Sebastian Stan), Falcon (Anthony Mackie), the Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen), Hawkeye (Jeremy Renner) and Avengers newcomer, Ant-Man (Paul Rudd.) 'The vis-dev group spent a lot of time locking down what the two sides - Tony's side and Cap's side - were going to look like," stated Dan DeLeeuw. "Once those looks were defined, we started developing the models with Industrial Light & Magic. 2 / 41 In addition to developing the looks of characters, the Marvel team - with heavy

input from the Russo brothers and producers Victoria Alonso and Kevin Feige - worked with The Third Floor in creating previsualizations for the film's key action sequences. "Early drafts for this movie had broad-brush descriptions of scenes," noted DeLeeuw. Plot points were detailed out, but a lot of the action had to be created in previs. Working from artwork and storyboards, we prevised an opening sequence in Lagos, a chase sequence in Bucharest, and then, of course, the big fight sequences, which included 'the splash panel,' which was the actual civil war fight between all the characters, and a final battle between Tony and Cap. The previs was a great creative tool for coming up with shots, and it was an inspiration for Joe and Anthony." P the different departments," explained DeLeeuw, "and then, when Joe and Anthony shot, they used the best ideas from each department. Then the footage went back to The Third Floor for postvis - so it came full circle in terms of how the ideas were developed, how they branched out in all of the other departments, and, finally, how those ideas came together in the end. The Third Floor's Gerardo Ramirez supervised both the previs and postvis work. Production was based at Pinewood Studios in Atlanta, with main unit shoots in Germany, as well. More exotic locations in Nigeria, Siberia and elsewhere fell largely to visual effects, but were grounded in plates and photography shot by Swen Gillberg and a globeCAPTAIN AMERICA 3 revis files were then sent to visual effects vendors, where they served as guidelines for final shots, and to the stunt team, led by stunt coordinator Sam Hargrave, informing the effects portions of stunt-vis. The previs went through all 3 / 41

trotting plate unit. "Swen and his plate unit went to Iceland," said DeLeeuw, "which stood CAPTAIN AMERICA 3I in for Siberia. They went to Puerto Rico, which doubled as Lagos. They also went to England, South America and upstate New York. Those plates really helped the feel of the film." "Due to rebates," added Gillberg, "most movies are made in the same few places - and so, it is easy for them to wind up looking the same. To give this film more production value, we had this plate unit go out to quite a few locations so that we could open it up and make Atlanta look like these exotic locales. The size of the plate unit contracted or expanded, depending on the location. Sometimes, it was just me, shooting backgrounds with a series of still cameras or with a Blackmagic digital camera to put motion in the background. At the other end of the extreme, our plate unit in Puerto Rico had a crew of 150 people, with two Alexa XT cameras, plus lidar and stills teams." The Puerto Rico setup included a drone and a helicopter for aerial photography. Supplied by Team5 Aerial System Rentals, the drone was large enough - eight feet long, with blades measuring about 16 inches - to handle a RED Epic Dragon camera, yet compact enough to fly into areas and at altitudes inaccessible by helicopter.iWe were able to fly it through the power lines for a shot in which Falcon's little sidekick, Redwing, flies down through the power lines and then follows him into the street," said Gillberg. "You couldn't do that with anything but a drone. The downside is that it involves a lot of FAA rules. You have to lock off a 250-foot radius around the drone, for example. So we hired a lot of PAs and traffic cops to lock down the streets of Puerto Rico." The Puerto Rico material served as backdrop for the film's opening sequence, which 4 / 41 has the Avengers in Lagos, staking out mercenaries intent on stealing a biological weapon

from the Institute for Infectious Diseases. Black Widow and the Scarlet Witch watch from an outdoor café, while Falcon conducts surveillance from atop a nearby skyscraper, and Captain America from inside a hotel room. What follows is the mercenaries' attack on the IFID, a chase through the streets of Lagos, and a final showdown in a marketplace, ending with a massive explosion. and plate photography, which compositing supervisor Jonathan Weber and his team used to surround Atlanta's Convention Center in shots of the mercenaries' truck approaching the IFID. "It was partly matte painting and partly 21⁄2D projection," said Rise visual effects supervisor Florian Gellinger. "We built some of the buildings in the background as smaller proxy houses, and then scattered those in Side Effects Houdini, and added CG vegetation using Speedtree." The truck impacts barriers at the IFID gate, causing it to roll. Though the truck was practical throughout - rolled on set by special effects supervisor Daniel Sudick and his team - Rise created the mechanical barriers as CG assets. We manipulated the CG barriers so that it looked as if the truck hit them," said Gellinger, "and then we simulated destruction effects in Houdini, with dust, dirt and debris breaking loose." Work inside the IFID compound included removing stunt rigs and adding CG toxic gas used by the mercenaries in their attack. Dan Sudick and his crew generated practical CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 he Lagos sequence's 300 shots were awarded to Rise Visual Effects Studios, which divided the work between its Berlin and Stuttgart facilities. Rise artists joined Swen Gillberg in Puerto Rico to conduct lidar surveys and shoot stills 5 / 41

CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 fog on set to create some ambient atmosphere, but the specific behavior and look of the gas was left to Rise.We ran Houdini fluid simulations to create the moving gas, with light scattering through the room and diffusing through the fog," Gellinger explained. "To make it interact correctly, we put the fluid simulations into the lidar-scanned room when we tracked in our cameras, and wherever we had a light source, the light would scatter nicely in the gas. We rendered all those gas shots as deep compositing setups so that we could manipulate and move the gas as necessary, and give it little touchups, going a little more opaque here or transparent there. Scarlet Witch uses her magic to contain the greenish-colored gas and blow it out of the building. The brief from the filmmakers was that Wanda's magic - what the crew dubbed the 'Wiggly Woo' - should appear to be strengthening in its power and intensity as Wanda learns to control it. "We went round and round with the look of that," recalled Swen Gillberg, who oversaw Rise's work on the sequence.iWe made it brighter, adding galaxy arms so that it would feel more powerful than what we saw in Age of Ultron. We added hot cores that vibrate as she exerts the poweri "The first step was to art-direct the gas to behave in a particular way," added Florian Gellinger, "and to follow a particular motion. Then, we had to design the Wiggly Woo wrapping around it. On top of that, we needed to light the gas with the Scarlet Witch eftect, which acts as a kind of light source - this reddish sparkle dust that creates volumetric lighting within the poisonous gas." Rise effects supervisor Andreas Giesen oversaw the Wiggly Woo effects, with Paul Schlie supervising the deep compositing of the gas at 6 / 41 the Stuttgart facility.

The mercenaries, bio-weapon in hand, are confronted by Black Widow, Falcon and Captain America as they attempt to escape the compound. Rise animation supervisor Alexander Schumann oversaw digi-double work for the fight scene, which was not as extensive as one might imagine, due to the stunt team's ability to perform dynamic fight moves in camera. "The stunt team was exceptional," stated Gellinger, "just the most bad-ass stuff we've ever witnessed. Sam Hargrave jumped down from a cherry picker without any wires, hit a couple of hard edges when he was falling down, and just stood up and walked away. All of the stunt work gave the fight scenes a raw touch that made them look very real. Even though there was some enhancement, starting off with a practical stunt gave us something really good to match to." Mackie and stunt performers on set. Then, for animated Falcon shots, Alexander Schumann rebuilt the Falcon asset provided by ILM from Ant-Man, based on the new costume and wing design. The upgraded model facilitated closeups on the character. ¿When Falcon uses his wing to shield himself," related Gellinger, "the wing is huge in frame; and so, it had to be much more detailed. We redesigned the wing parts into smaller mechanical pieces, and then made those mechanical pieces work in unison when they folded back into the backpacki The wings' feather-like plates were made to look as if they were made of a transparCAPTAIN AMERICA 3 t one point in the fight, Falcon uses his wing to shield himself from gunfire. Working with costume designer Judianna Makovsky, Legacy Effects built Falcon's backpack, wrist gauntlets, shoulder pads and leg shields, all worn by Anthony 7 / 41

ent fabric; but, rather than simulate the cloth wings, Rise artists animated them by hand. CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 "Simulation didn't give us the flexibility we needed in the wings," explained Gellinger, "so, instead, we first animated the frame, and then did a second pass, animating the cloth as blend shapes. After that, we made some adjustments on the frame, the animators flexing and bending it as needed - but not so far that it looked like rubber. By going with full animation, we could manipulate the wings in all the necessary ways. Cantina Creative, which has created HUDs and other graphics for all of the Marvel films to date, contributed features of Falcon's updated design. Falcon has some cool tech in this movie," said Cantina Creative visual effects supervisor Alan Torres, "including his own little HUD, which has a more military look than Iron Man's. One of the words the Russos always used to describe the graphics was 'grounded.' The aesthetics of our work throughout this movie, including Falcon's tech, had to feel grounded in today's reality." Another new Falcon feature is the Redwing drone he deploys to give him additional firepower. Working from artwork generated by Ryan Meinderding and his team, Legacy Effects built the Redwing as a stationary prop that fit inside Falcon's backpack. "We made one Falcon backpack that had Redwing in it," noted Legacy supervisor Lindsay Macgowan, 'and one that didn't. We also made a separate lighting reference prop - again, working with the design team to make sure it fit within the negative space of the backpack." Rise used the Legacy Effects prop as reference for its Redwing digital model, working out its mechanics in the final rig. A subsequent chase through the streets of Lagos leads to a marketplace, an Atlanta 8 / 41 set which Rise CG supervisor Oliver Schulz extended using the Puerto Rico photography V

and scans. "The marketplace became a lot bigger," said Florian Gellinger, "so we tripled CAPTAIN AMERICA 3I or quadrupled the number of market stalls, adding simulated cloud volumes to represent barbeque and fire smoke moving across the environment. We also added a lot of vegetation - palm trees and other foliage and trees we'd seen in Puerto Rico - and simulated a crowd walking amongst the CG market stalls." Rise artists simulated the crowd in Houdini. i Our effects supervisor, Andreas Giesen, had just released a tutorial on how to control a crowd properly in Houdini, so he was the guy to do all of this crowd worki In addition to extending the set, Rise altered a Federal building in Atlanta and moved it closer to the marketplace, facilitating the story point of its coming down in the explosion that occurs when Crossbones (Frank Grillo) blows himself up, forcing Scarlet Witch to thrust him toward the structure, away from the crowd. "In order to blow up the building later," said Gellinger, "we had to build a detailed replica, which included all the sub-layers of wiring and rebar you'd find behind the building facade. We also furnished the offices with desks, chairs and computers - dressing you'd see inside, illuminated by the fire of the explosion." Rise added another apartment building adjacent to the Federal building, built from lidar scans and photographs from Puerto Rico.iThose two big buildings served to contain the market," Gellinger said. "From a story point of view, it was important to Joe and Anthony to show that Scarlet Witch has no other choice than to throw Crossbones into one of those buildings when he blows himself up - because she doesn't have anywhere else to throw him. It needed to be a confined space. This whole movie is about people getting 9 / 41 hurt through the actions of superheroes; and so, it was important to show that she

doesn't have an alternative. Rise realized the building destruction by running pyrotechnic, dust and smoke simulations in Houdini. S "We had to 'youthenize' Robert Downey Jr. for this scene," said Dan DeLeeuw, "which would have been challenging enough; but then, the Russos decided to do the whole scene as a oner, so that it wouldn't feel like a cut movie scene, but rather like a playback of a person's memory. Further complicating the memory scene, crews shot it in an Atlanta house too small to accommodate motion control equipment, which would have facilitated the seaming of separate passes. "It basically became poor man's motion control, just doing a lot of takes of Tony's younger self waking up on a couch and walking across the room, and then filming present-day Robert appearing in the doorway behind him and coming forward to address the MIT audience. Animal Logic married those two passes together, and digitally repaired the room where the two passes didn't quite line up. The final shot, which peels back to reveal the domestic scene as a hologram, ran a whopping 4,000 frames long. "It goes on for a very long time," noted Animal Logic visual effects supervisor Paul Butterworth, "as if you are seeing the scene through a projection system. We did the holographic reveal in that shot, as well as in the following shot, when you realize that Tony Stark isn't in that lounge room at all, but rather on stage at MIT. The whole reveal is subtle, mainly because they didn't want to distract from CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 tateside, we find Tony Stark in a large theater, presenting MIT students with new holographic technology capable of generating photoreal representations of memories. In the demonstration, a 21-year-old Tony interacts with his parents. 10 / 41

Robert's performance." CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 Animal Logic also filled the MIT theater seats. 'They had the front row of the theater that was in-camera," said Butterworth, "but that wasn't enough. So we did a casting call at Animal Logic. I said, 'Hey, if you want to star in Captain America, come on down.' And we were inundated with responses within fifteen minutes. In the end, we shot 80 people, individually, sitting in a chair, clapping, and then doing a standing ovation. Then we put them on cards to fill the theater. It's all Animal Logic staff filling the back rows. Youthening effects on Robert Downey Jr. went to Lola VFX, which has perfected the art; but, even for Lola, the nearly three-minute-long shot presented special challenges. "Because it was so long," said Lola visual effects supervisor Trent Claus, "it was the equivalent of doing 25 or 30 shots. There were no cuts in it, so we couldn't use the usual tricks to hide transitions. Also, the young Tony is right there in the foreground, not hidden at all, and there were a lot of 180-degree turns, which complicated our process. We never want considerations about our work to hinder a performance, but the turns and scale changes in one long take definitely made this more complexi Lola's facial de-aging process started with photographing an appropriately aged double in the company's light rig, re-creating Downey Jr.'s original performance. Lola had done the casting of the double at its facility, looking for as close a match to the young Robert Downey Jr. as possible. "We look for matching bone structure," Claus explained, "matching creases around the mouth so that when he talked or smiled, the skin in that area would behave the same as Robert's. When shooting the double, Lola artists re-created 11 / 41 the on-set lighting exactly so they could ascertain what the facial features would do in

that specific lighting situation. "We had to see how the neck would react when he turned his head, how the cheeks would look in that sort of light. We were looking at not only the shape of things, but also how those shapes interacted with the lighti fore." Lola divided the shot into 15 distinct pieces of performance, had the double in the light rig re-create each of those 15 beats, and then spliced them back together. Most often, Lola artists used the resulting imagery as reference for their 2D resculpting of Robert Downey's face; but, in some cases, they had to actually track in small areas of the double's face to achieve the desired result. 'There is a buildup of skin on the jawline and chin that happens as you age, and that is very difficult to remove in a 2D process. So, we often pulled in those areas from the double, doing skin grafts, essentially, on certain trouble areas. We tightened the upper eyelids and removed wrinkles - enough to make him look younger, but not so much that it looked synthetic. That's where the artistry comes in, finding that fine line. In addition to the facial work, Lola executed some subtle modifications to Downey Jr.'s body to make him look 30 years younger, an illusion the actor aided during his performance by purposefully holding himself and moving as a younger man. Meanwhile, the nefarious plot that sets the film's civil war in motion transpires at a Hydra facility, where Baron Zemo (Daniel Brühl) makes use of a Red Book he has stolen, CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 gain, the extended length of the shot made the process more challenging. "It was just too long a period for someone to mimic the performancei said Claus, 'so we had to chop it into pieces, which was something we'd never faced be12 / 41

CAPTAIN AMERICA 3I reading code words that move a restrained Winter Soldier to break free and escape the compound. Luma Pictures executed shots featuring CG restraints and a CG cage, and also did some CG torso and arm replacements to create interactions with Winter Soldier's mechanical arm. Luma also extended the interior Hydra set, the walls of which the production crew had lined with sheets of gray material in extension areas, creating a base for final, more textured digital concrete walls. "I'd never encountered that before," recounted Luma Pictures visual effects supervisor Vincent Cirelli. "It was a really interesting technique because it meant we didn't have to do a full CG render. All we rendered out were textural details, shadows and highlights on the concrete, and then we just layered those details over these gray sheets. In the end, it looked just like concrete - and it was a lot easier than if we'd had to do a complete CG concrete replacement on an existing brick wall, for example. Also, the gray cloth behind the actors meant that we didn't have to do much painting around them. We were able to just use rotos and luma-keys to get the characters against the concrete. It worked really well." The story then cuts to the Avengers' taskforce headquarters in upstate New York, where they learn of the 'Sokovia Accords,' drafted as a measure to exert tighter control on the superheroes' activities. For an aerial reveal of the compound, artists at Double Negative blended photography of the Porsche Experience Center in Atlanta - which also served for interiors — and the Sainsbury Center for Visual Arts in Norwich, England with an aerial plate from the Hudson River Valley in New York. Double Negative also added synthetic structures. "We had to create that whole compound, with interconnecting roads," 13 / 41 recounted Double Negative visual effects supervisor Peter Jopling. "It was principally 21⁄2D.

We had a tight time frame, and it was only one shot; and so, we didn't want to work up three big assets for that environment. Instead, we went with a DMP projection solutioni head and hands, dotted with tracking markers. That plate then went to Lola, which implemented effects to give the character his metallic, geometric look. Lola didn't create a CG face," said Dan DeLeeuw, "but rather an enhanced version of Paul's face, smoothing his skin and adding appliances that made him look more like a sculpted robot. The great thing about this approach is that we were able to retain Paul's performance. "We'd learned quite a lot on Age of Ultron in the creation of Vision's head," added Trent Claus. iWe were able to take all the models, shaders and animation rigs we had built for the previous film and improve upon them for this one. In that respect, it went much more smoothly on this movie - even though we had more Vision shots, and more shots of Vision talking to other characters, with a lot of subtle emotion going on in his face. The intricacies of a facial performance, the little twitches of the eyebrows, half smiles and smirks, are very difficult to duplicate in full CG, but they work very well with this process, where we are merging the original performance with a synthetic head, rather than entirely replacing iti As a full-fledged member of the Avengers, Vision would feature far more prominently in Civil War, and his super-powers would be more clearly on display. We kept his look CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 mong the residents at the headquarters is Vision (Paul Bettany), the bio-Vibranium hybrid introduced in Age of Ultron. As he had for that film, Bettany portrayed the red-hued Vision on set wearing prosthetics and red-colored makeup on his 14 / 41

basically the same," said Dan DeLeeuw, "but we added behaviors and powers that weren't CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 evident in the previous film, such as his ability to phase. He can shift his density, so he can become lighter than air - which enables him to walk through walls - or he can become so dense that he can withstand a lot of damage in fights. There are limitations to this density-shifting power, however. He can't fight when he's light, and he can't fly when he is too dense. So, in a way, we were constraining his powers, even as we were exploring them more fully." Development of the phasing effects was shared by Lola, ILM and Double Negative, all three of which first referenced Vision's phasing powers as they were illustrated in the comic books - a fog-filled transparency within the borders of his body. ¿We wanted to do something more sophisticated than that," noted Peter Jopling, "but it wasn't clear, at first, what that look would be. It couldn't look biological or anatomical, because Vision isn't made of flesh and bones; and exposing internal organs can get icky. We realized that since Vision can move his mass to another dimension, we had to expand our horizons as to what the phasing looked like. Transparency was still an element of it, and then we refined it, and wound up with something that was simple, yet elegant." Starting with concept art, Double Negative artists worked in Side Effects Houdini to create its phasing effects, which were finally designed to look part-organic, and partelectronic. "We thought of it as sort of an organic circuit board," said Jopling. "If we went too electronic, it quickly got into Tron territory; and so, we applied more of an organic structure to it." 15 / 41 Lola also took on some Vision phasing shots, including one in which Vision phases

through the wall of a bedroom. "It was an interesting scene because he's not in his superCAPTAIN AMERICA 3I hero suit, but rather in a black sweater," commented Trent Claus. "In showing transparency and dimensionality in the body, the super suit is very useful because it has lines of armor that we can outline. With the sweater, it was almost like a black void; and so, how do you show that he's not just a two-dimensional character walking through the wall, that he has form and dimension? That was a hurdle to overcome." Lola returned to the birth of Vision sequence in Age of Ultron for inspiration. iWe saw him naked in that scene," said Claus, "and he had a design covering his naked body. From that, we determined that, underneath the sweater, he still had some design elements on his body, and some hints of the super suit that he's created for himself. That allowed us to cheat in some dimension. When he walked through the wall, he was actually impacting that surface, and we showed that with a bit of an electric spark. We also incorporated some plasma dots, similar to what they had used in the comic books. Jack Kirby, the famous comic book artist, was known for drawing plasma bubbles around things that were happening. It's subtle, but we tried to create some of those as a nod to the comics." Despite disagreement within their ranks, the Avengers join luminaries in Vienna for the signing of the Sokovia Accords. Production shot a building in Berlin to represent the U.N. facility, and then Double Negative composited it with aerial views of Vienna, created, in part, as a synthetic environment. The original idea was that we'd just use photography for the exterior environment," said Peter Jopling, "but it became apparent that the 16 / 41 photography wasn't going to be enough, and so we built this whole complex of glass-

fronted buildings, in part to get an array of proper reflections. To make it look completely real, this was the only way to do it - building the environment, and putting the right camera in there to get the correct depth of field. It worked out brilliantly, because once we got through the initial build stage, it made the actual comping of the shots much more straightforward. "The bottom floors blow up, and then the face of the building comes down. The tricky part was designing this blast so that it could kill the Wakanda king, but not kill everybody in the room. It couldn't be so over the top that nobody could survive it." For destruction shots inside the building, Double Negative replaced a practical explosion executed by Dan Sudick's special effects crew on set. There was a great pyrotechnic that blew up the lectern where T'Chaka does his speech in front of the auditorium, said Peter Jopling, iand that pyrotechnic element showed us what that explosion would look like in that room - even though, in the film, the explosion is initiated outside the building. Those photographic cues were incredibly useful." An exterior shot reveals the explosion, with a huge fireball and clouds of smoke rising between the buildings. A drone plate shot on location became the foundation for Double Negative's destruction effects, implemented in Houdini. News footage of the disaster implicates Winter Soldier - aka, Bucky Barnes, Captain CAPTAIN AMERICA 3I uring the ceremony, a bomb-laden news van pulls up and detonates, causing a huge blast to go off in the building, killing Wakanda's king, T'Chaka (John Kani). "We based the look of this explosion on improvised bombs," said Dan DeLeeuw. 17 / 41

CAPTAIN AMERICA 3 America's longtime friend — as the bomber. To ensure that Bucky is taken into custody, alive and well, Cap seeks him out at his apartment in Bucharest. Trixter delivered 330 shots for the Bucharest sequence: a scene in Bucky's apartment, a rooftop fight between Bucky and Black Panther - T'Chaka's son, T'Challa, who dons the superhero costume to avenge his father's death - and a chase through the city's freeway tunnels. Production shot an apartment scuffle between Cap and Bucky on a set in Atlanta. Across the Sea of Time BY JOE FORDHAM •n 2010, Walt Disney Pictures' Alice in Wonderland provided an alternative take on Lewis Carroll's fantasy classics Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking Glass (And What Alice Found There). Filmmaker Tim Burton and screenwriter Linda Woolverton depicted 'Underland' as a half-remembered childhood fantasy realm, which Alice (Mia Wasikowska) revisits on the eve of her wedding to an unwanted suitor. Burton, production designer Robert Stromberg and visual effects supervisor Ken Ralston created strange landscapes and creatures using performers in greenscreen sets coupled with digital animation - the majority accomplished at Sony Pictures Imageworks. The film went on to receive Academy Awards for achievements in costume design and art direction, and an Oscar nomination for visual effects. The conundrum facing the makers of a follow-up adventure was what, if any, of Carroll's fantasy remained for adaptation after the fever dream of the previous film. 'Tim Burton and Robert Stromberg had a fantastic visioni observed director James Bobin. They had created a very beautiful Victorian Gothic look, with Tim's own stylistic choices. 1 / 24 I'd always found it interesting that the Alice books appeared at the high point of the Vic-

ALICE 2 torian Gothic period. I wanted to keep that alive in the sequel, so the world remained recognizable. But the great joy of the new story was that it involved concepts of time travel. The idea that Underland was relatively unexplored, other than the places we'd visited in the first movie, allowed us freedom to show how the world looked 20 or 40 years ago, and then we visited other places as the story developedi New environments described in Linda Woolverton's screenplay, Alice Through the Looking Glass, included the Outlands, where the egomaniacal Red Queen (Helena Bonham Carter) had been banished since Alice (Wasikowska) defeated the Queen's fearsome Jabberwocky and freed Underland from tyranny. Alice finds her old accomplice, the Mad Hatter (Johnny Depp), even more demented than before, living in his childhood village of Witzend, and seeks the assistance of Time (Sacha Baron Cohen), an eccentric overlord who holds the power to undo Hatter's misfortunes by influencing the chronology of Underland. The new concepts drew on traditions of Carrollian absurdist logic.iI've always thought of Lewis Carroll as a satirist," said Bobin. "His satire and surrealism aren't far from the Monty Python humor that we saw in the 1970s. It's a tone of English humor that threads through the history of comedy. I wanted to bring that to the film, maintaining continuity with the world that the previous film had created, but taking it to new and interesting places in terms of feel and color, with a slightly different comedic tone. Production designer Dan Hennah spearheaded the design initiative with a team of conceptual artists that included veterans of Tim Burton's film. Ken Ralston again guided 2 / 24 visual effects, working with Sony Pictures Imageworks visual effects supervisor Jay Redd

and animation supervisor Troy Saliba at Imageworks' studio in Culver City, California, ALICE 2 while digital effects supervisors Theo Bialek and Craig Wentworth led Imageworks' work in Vancouver. The production set up operations at Shepperton Studios in England, where construction teams erected Underland environments backed by bluescreen.iEverybody who worked on the first Alice film voted to go blue instead of green this time," commented visual effects producer Mike Chambers. "Greenscreen is perhaps preferable in the digital realm for dealing with mattes, but when you're surrounded by green 24 hours a day for months on end, it's a little tougher on the psyche. So Ken and Jay said, 'Blue is fine.' Otherwise, it was a similar approach to the last film, with big blue stages and blue standin props, and limited location shooting for real-world scenes." To plan fantasy realms, the production's in-house previsualization supervisor Rpin Suwannath developed 3D animatics, and Halon Entertainment previsualization supervisor Tefft Smith developed postvis, which allowed Imageworks to plot combinations of liveaction and digital animation, building on techniques gleaned from the previous film. What I learned working on the last film," remarked Ken Ralston, "was that it was most helpful to get answers before we got too deep into the visual effects, using concept art and previs to extract information from the director. We still went round and round on some designs into postproduction, but it was important to plan as much as possible because the show was so huge.
